RagShortTexts: The Wettin dynasty governed Meissen and Thuringia, leveraging silver mines and eastern.

Variants.Content: The Wettin dynasty ruled the Margraviate of Meissen and the landgraviate of Thuringia, a country of forest, river and mining hills along the Elbe. Under Margrave Henry the Illustrious, the family drew wealth from the silver veins near Freiberg, whose mines paid for the armour, the castles and the hired soldiers that secured the eastern frontier. The Ostsiedlung had opened the eastern forests to German settlers, and the margraves used charters to organise new villages and their taxes. Imperial loyalty and careful marriages kept the dynasty in favour with the emperor, while the frontier against Bohemia and the Slavic lands demanded constant readiness. Mining revenue let the margraves hire mercenaries, build stone keeps on the rivers and pay for the mounted knights who made their rule secure.

Meissen silver paid the wages of mercenary crossbowmen and the upkeep of fortified bridges on the Elbe. Each mining charter and each toll was recorded in the margrave's accounts, so that the family could meet any baronial challenge with ready coin. Ready coin meant the margrave could settle a feud before it reached the field.
